item.text: I’m adding only remembered omissions, with verse-level continuations where they add a distinct detail. I won’t inspect or otherwise read the saved file.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/103_1/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.40.14	Joseph asks the released cupbearer to remember him	The commentary notes Joseph's request to be remembered and the cupbearer's later forgetting; Genesis gives the request itself, asking the cupbearer to mention him to Pharaoh and bring him out of prison.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.105.18	Joseph confined in fetters	The commentary places Joseph's waiting in prison; the psalm retells his story as feet bound in fetters until the promised time, giving the confinement a bodily image.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.105.19	Joseph tested until his word comes true	The commentary arranges Joseph's prison years around delayed remembrance and eventual release; the psalm says the word of the Lord tested Joseph until what he had said came to pass, interpreting the delay as a trial.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.29	Seven years of abundance forecast	The commentary follows Joseph's reading of Pharaoh's dream as a calendar of plenty and scarcity; Genesis predicts seven years of great abundance throughout Egypt, specifying the productive span.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.30	Seven famine years follow	The commentary's Joseph narrative turns from years of yield to years of hardship; Genesis forecasts seven years of famine after the abundance, making the saved grain's time horizon explicit.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.31	The plenty is forgotten in famine	The commentary says the hard years consume what was stored; Genesis adds that the famine is so severe that the former plenty is no longer remembered, a sharper account of yield erased by loss.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.47	The land produces abundantly during the good years	The commentary follows the movement from productive years to preserved grain; Genesis says the land yields abundantly through the seven years, the harvest that makes Joseph's storage possible.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.56	Joseph opens the storehouses in famine	The commentary ends Joseph's cycle with renewed access to produce after scarcity; Genesis says Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain during the famine, showing reserve released when need arrives.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.4	Those who trample the needy	The commentary's garden owners plan to keep the poor from their crop; Amos addresses people who trample the needy and bring the poor to an end, naming the injustice that the garden scene dramatizes.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.6	Poor people traded for silver while wheat is sold	The commentary contrasts hoarded produce with giving; Amos condemns buyers who acquire the poor for silver and sell even wheat refuse, making grain control an instrument of exploitation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.15.7	Do not close the hand against the poor	The commentary describes holding a gift back and excluding the poor from a garden; Deuteronomy forbids hardening the heart or shutting the hand against a poor kinsman, a direct ethical counterpoint.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.15.8	Open the hand to meet another's need	The commentary says squeezing can let its extract flow as generosity; Deuteronomy commands opening the hand and lending enough for the poor person's need, making release the ethical response to scarcity.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.15.10	Give freely without a grudging heart	The commentary contrasts a generous person with one who withholds or reclaims a gift; Deuteronomy commands giving without regret and promises blessing for the work, joining openhandedness to fruitful outcome.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.19	A forgotten sheaf left for the poor	The commentary's owners plan to keep a garden's entire yield from the poor; Deuteronomy says a forgotten sheaf must remain for the stranger, orphan, and widow, applying release to grain harvest.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ruth.2.15	Ruth allowed to glean among the sheaves	The commentary's garden owners bar the poor from entering; Boaz tells his workers to let Ruth glean even among the sheaves and not reproach her, reversing exclusion in a concrete harvest scene.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ruth.2.16	Extra grain deliberately left for Ruth	The commentary treats a crop's extract as a gift that may either flow or be retained; Boaz orders handfuls pulled from the bundles and left for Ruth, making generosity exceed mere permission to glean.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ruth.2.20	A close relative as guardian and redeemer	The commentary says ancestry and kinship can be a refuge; Naomi identifies Boaz as a near kinsman and redeemer, where family connection becomes practical protection and provision.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:15	The day is short, work is abundant, and the master presses	The commentary calls late afternoon the point when work is nearly done and time for unfinished tasks narrows; this saying makes the same pressure explicit through a short day, much work, and an urgent master.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.12.7	An oath measures the time until oppression ends	The commentary opens with an oath on time and leaves the promised verdict just beyond the verse; Daniel's angel swears by the living God and gives a measured period whose end coincides with the breaking of the holy people's power.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.12.12	Blessed is the one who waits to the appointed days	The commentary includes delayed arrival, a fleeting moment, and patience through hard years; Daniel blesses the person who waits and reaches the stated number of days, linking endurance to a measured end.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.10.6	An oath that there will be no more delay	The commentary hears both a broad age and a late, shortened interval in asr; Revelation's angel swears that there will be no more delay before the mystery is completed, joining oath, waiting, and time's end.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Heb.3.18	The oath is directed at the disobedient	The commentary places an oath before a verdict of loss; Hebrews continues its reading of Psalm 95 by identifying those excluded from rest as the disobedient, specifying why the sworn exclusion occurs.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Heb.3.19	Unbelief prevents entry	The commentary moves from a general human loss to an exception for believers; Hebrews says the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief, giving the faith contrast a precise interpretive role.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Heb.4.7	The present day is still called Today	The commentary treats a named time as a threshold before action becomes too late; Hebrews says God again appoints a day called Today and warns against hardening the heart, reading the old oath as a present opportunity.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.8.35	Prayer when heaven is shut and rain withheld	The commentary connects prayer at a set time with clouds, rain, and crop yield; Solomon prays for the people when heaven is closed and there is no rain, linking drought, prayer, repentance, and renewed provision.
weak	tevrat	soydas	WLC:1Kgs.8.35	Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified	The package table marks Hebrew עצר as a possible sound correspondence to Arabic ع ص ر; Solomon's prayer describes heaven being shut so rain stops, a relevant restraint of the rain that the commentary links to yield, without proving cognacy.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.142.6	God is refuge in the cave prayer	The commentary treats a cave as refuge for people whose time is hidden from them; Psalm 142's superscription places David in a cave, and the cited verse calls God his refuge and portion while he is in distress.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.18	Fleeing for refuge and holding fast to hope	The commentary joins seeking shelter with clinging tightly to a person or place; Hebrews describes people who have fled for refuge to seize the hope set before them, bringing refuge and grasping together.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Dan.6.10	Daniel prays three times each day under threat	The commentary describes believers praying at the day's edges; Daniel continues praying three times daily toward Jerusalem despite a decree that endangers his life, showing fixed prayer times maintained under pressure.
medium	incil	motif	Didache 8:3	The Lord's Prayer said three times daily	The commentary names the afternoon prayer and describes morning-evening devotion; the Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, evidence of a timed daily discipline.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.10.3	Cornelius prays at the ninth hour	The commentary leaves open the afternoon-prayer sense of asr; Acts places Cornelius in prayer at the ninth hour when he sees an angel, a distinct Christian scene of late-day devotion.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.13.35	Evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning	The commentary lets one unqualified time-name span an afternoon, an era, or a fleeting interval; Jesus lists the night watches and warns that the master may come at any one of them, making readiness depend on an unknown hour.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.141.3	Prayer rises like incense	The commentary describes perfume swelling and rising behind a passing person; the psalm asks that prayer rise like incense, a distinct connection to the commentary's scent image apart from this verse's evening-offering detail.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Song.4.16	Wind releases garden spices and fruit	The commentary brings together wind, garden produce, and fragrance carried after movement; the Song calls on the winds to blow through a garden so its spices flow and its fruits can be eaten, joining those images in one scene.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.7.1	Fragrance set beside the day of death	The commentary follows a woman's perfume trail into a reflection on what remains after someone passes and also makes asr a life's closing time; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than fragrant oil and the day of death better than birth.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.11.6	Sow in the morning and keep working in the evening	The commentary says the late day leaves little time for work still undone and connects time with uncertain yield; Ecclesiastes commands sowing in the morning and not letting the hand rest in the evening because the outcome is unknown.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.2	Light darkens as old age approaches	The commentary hears afternoon's fading light alongside the end of a human life; Ecclesiastes depicts sun, light, moon, and stars darkening as the days of aging arrive, giving that decline a bodily and cosmic image.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.4.6	A life poured out as departure nears	The commentary treats squeezing as extracting a life-giving essence and asr as the close of a lifespan; Paul says he is already being poured out as a libation and that the time of his departure has come.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.52	Transformation in a moment at the last trumpet	The commentary holds long ages beside the instant and says a whole lifetime can shrink to a small part of a day; Paul places the change of the dead in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.12.24	A grain dies and bears much fruit	The commentary describes grain protected in its husk through scarcity and later used for food; Jesus says a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit, making fruitful release rather than protected storage the condition of abundance.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.9	Harvest comes in due time to those who do not give up	The commentary links the final patience-word to waiting through lean years for stored grain to yield; Paul urges continued good work because harvest comes at the proper time if one does not grow weary.
medium	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 3:6	The tested righteous are refined like gold	The commentary says time's pressure extracts an essence and connects patience with a bitter extract; Wisdom pictures the tested righteous as gold tried in a furnace and accepted like a burnt offering, interpreting pressure as refinement.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.4.18	A material gift is a fragrant offering	The commentary makes pressed yield an image of generosity and perfume a good trace left behind; Paul calls the Philippians' delivered gift a fragrant offering, joining concrete giving with lingering fragrance.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.2.14	The fragrance of knowledge spreads everywhere	The commentary describes a scent rising and trailing after movement; Paul says God spreads the fragrance of knowledge through the apostles everywhere, turning a passing procession into a lasting trail.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.2.15	Aroma received differently by the saved and perishing	The commentary contrasts a good trace left behind with destructive dust and loss; Paul says the same aroma is associated with those being saved and those perishing, adding opposed outcomes to the scent image.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.15.25	Bitter water becomes drinkable	The commentary's poem imagines water itself as the thing choking the speaker, with no rescuing sip left; at Marah, God shows Moses a tree and the bitter water becomes sweet, a contrasting scene where the obstructing water is made into relief.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.13.8	The gardener asks for one more year	The commentary's old garden owner loses his final yield when there is no time or strength to plant again; Jesus' gardener asks for another year to dig and fertilize the barren tree, making time an opportunity for restoration.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.21	Rich toward God rather than oneself	The commentary contrasts generous outflow with stored yield kept from others; Jesus concludes that the farmer who stores goods for himself is not rich toward God, giving the accumulation scene its ethical verdict.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.26	A fixed chasm makes relief impossible	The commentary's thirsty speaker has no remaining rescue sip; Abraham says a great chasm is fixed between the two places and no one can cross, explaining why the rich man's requested relief cannot arrive.
medium	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:15	The master is pressing and the day's work is unfinished	The commentary calls late afternoon the point when time for unfinished work narrows; this saying names a short day, abundant work, and a pressing master, spelling out the pressure of limited time.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.13.8	A second reason: the remaining year can still bear fruit	The commentary's storm destroys an aging owner's garden when he can no longer replant; the gardener's request for one additional year makes a specific counter-image of a remaining season used to recover fruit.
EOF"
